Adhyātma Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Upaniṣads are the treasurehouse of the spiritual knowledge of India. They have been accepted and venerated as basic scriptures by most of the religio-philosophical schools of India. Every philo-sopher or religious reformer has taken pains to show that his views are rooted in the Upaniṣadic traditions, or at least, do not go against them. Even the non-Hindu and non-Indian savants have heaped praises on their enlightened views.
The ten उपनिषद्स् on which शङ्कर (A.

-820) wrote commentaries have universally been accepted as the more ancient, more authentic and authoritative. The Adhyātma Upaniṣad, though outside this list, still, breathes the spirit of the more ancient and the major उपनिषद्स्.
Since the printed texts give the śāntimantra as ‘pūrṇamadaḥ ...’ it is to be surmised that it belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda. The last verse of the Upaniṣad declares that it was first revealed to the sage Apāntaratamas who taught it to ब्रह्मा. ब्रह्मा gave it to Ghora अङ्गिरस् who in turn transmitted the same to रैक्व. रैक्व passed it on to राम and राम revealed it to all the living beings.
The teaching itself has been designated as ‘nirvāṇānuśāsanam’ (‘command concerning final emancipation’).
The text consists of 70 verses, all in the śloka metre, and has not been divided into sub-sections. But there is a method and order in the dealing of the subject matter. It starts with the description of the antarātman, the Innermost Self, the same as Adhyātman, (hence the name Adhyātma Upaniṣad) who exists in all things and beings controlling them from within, but whom none of them knows. He has also been called ‘Nārāyaṇa’ here (verse 1). After declaring that the sense of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ with regard to the body and the senses which are अनात्मन् or non-Self, arises due to अध्यास or superimposition by इग्नोरन्चे, the Upaniṣad exhorts us to get rid of this अध्यास by being devoted to ब्रह्मन् and through discrimination. The line of arguments to be pursued in this is practically the same as in Advaita Vedānta (v. 2-11). This is followed by a description of the आत्मन्-ब्रह्मन् principle as the one without a second, and without internal distinctions. The disciple is asked to see It as his own Self (v. 12-27). Renunciation leads to intuitive knowledge which results in the withdrawal of the मिन्द् into itself. Resting it on the आत्मन्, one attains infinite peace and joy or realization. This is the next topic (v. 28 and 29). Then, the identity between the जीव (individual सोउल्) and ब्रह्मन् (the Cosmic सोउल्) is shown by negating the accidental characteristics like association with the मिन्द् and the māyā-power (v.30-32) followed by a delineation of the three sādhanās or practices, śravaṇa (hearing), मनन (reflection) and निदिध्यासन (meditation) resulting in समाधि (superconscious experience) (v. 33-35). Then, there is the description of ‘dharma-megha-समाधि,’ ‘the समाधि which results in कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन्’ (v. 36-43). This is followed by a nice pen-picture of the jīvanmukta, one who is liberated even while living in the body (v. 44-47). He is never affected by the vicissitudes of life and is ever in equipoise. Then the Upaniṣad says that the knowledge of the आत्मन् destroys all the previously accumulated karmas, except the prārabdha-कर्म which has already begun to fructify. It can be exhausted only through experience. However, the liberated सोउल् is unaffected by it (v. 48-60). It ends with a poetic description of the personal experience of the jīvanmukta (v. 61-69).
This Upaniṣad is sometimes called Turīyātīta अवधूत Upaniṣad also.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa
------------------------------------------
Hindu life will lose all its meaning and charm without राम and कृष्ण, the two colossuses that have strode the Hindu heart for the last few millennia. If the Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmikī has been the basis on which the राम personality has been built up, no less important are its numerous imitations and adoptions that have kept alive the राम cult and the राम community leading to the development of Rāmālogy. Perhaps, one of the most important Sanskrit works of this type is the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa which is very popular in North India, not only among the devotees of राम but also among the Vedāntins. In fact, it is this work that provided तुलसीदास with the inspiration to compose his immortal work, the Rāmacaritmānasa.
Though depicted as a part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, respected as a canonical work of the Vaiṣṇavas and begun in the Tantra style of conversation between शिव महादेव and पार्वती, scholars ascribe it to the period 14th-15th cent. A.D. Nothing is known of the author, though the राम tradition believes it to be वेदव्यास since it is said to be an integral part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Like its original source, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa also has seven kāṇḍas or books, named in the same manner, except for the sixth, the Yuddhakāṇḍa, which is sometimes designated Laṅkākāṇḍa. The total number of verses is 4200 spread over 65 sargas or chapters. Written in mellifluous Sanskrit, the work admirably sums up the main events of the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि omitting only the minor details, or descriptions of war and nature. On the other hand new material pertaining to Vedānta philo-sophy, the cult of भक्ति in general and राम-भक्ति in particular and several hymns in praise of राम have been liberally added.
A few of the changes and innovations made, departing from the original may be noted here: The major alteration in the facts of the story is the introduction of a shadow सीता throughout the period of her abduction, the real सीता having disappeared into the fire just before the golden deer episode. She re-emerges from the fire at the end of the war when the shadow सीता enters into it. The whole drama is preplanned and enacted at the bidding of राम himself (vide 3.7). Other alterations though minor in nature, are: the earth accompanies the gods in the form of a cow (1.2); सुमित्रा gets more of the sacred pudding than कौसल्या and कैकेयी (1.3); अहल्या after being cursed by her husband, the sage गौतम, becomes a stone (1.5); रावण treats सीता with the respect due to a मोथेर् (3.7.65); राम establishes a शिवलिङ्ग at the site of the bridge to लङ्का (

-2).
Coming to the additions to Vālmikī’s story, five paurāṇic episodes need be mentioned: the stories about वाल्मीकि himself (2.6), शुक (6.5) and Kālanemi (6.6) who warn रावण about राम’s divinity and the need to propitiate him, Vālī and सुग्रीव (7.3). The dialogue between रावण and Sanatkumāra is another addition (7.3).
But the major contribution of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa lies in its casting of राम in the role of a spiritual teacher and in the several exquisite hymns sung in praise of राम. There are four occasions when राम assumes the role of the teacher and gives philosophic disquisitions. In response to लक्ष्मण’s questions on three different occasions he teaches know-ledge, devotion, detachment (vide 3.4), methods of worship (4.4) and the way of emancipation (7.5). In reply to कौसल्या’s query, he teaches the three yogas of कर्म, ज्ञान and भक्ति (7.7).
The well-known Rāmagītā is part of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and is the teaching given to लक्ष्मण on the last occasion already referred to (7.5). It contains a rather strong dose of Advaita Vedānta though couched in beautiful poetry. In fact some scholars feel that this Rāmagītā and Rāmahṛdaya (1.1) were independent works incorporated later into this Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
As regards the laudatory hymns, we find quite a good number of them: by ब्रह्मा (1.2; 6.13), कौसल्या (1.3), नारद (2.1), वाल्मीकि (2.6), जटायु (3.8), विभीषण (6.6) and all the gods (6.15).
However the real contribution of this work is in its repeatedly propounding the doctrine that राम is ब्रह्मन् the Absolute and that सीता is his Māyāśakti or प्रकृति, thereby raising the personality of राम to the highest level and providing a firm base to the cult of राम. No occasion that gives a chance to do this is missed. Not only sages, gods and devotees, but even the enemies of Rāma—not excepting रावण himself !—recognise his divinity and divine mission. Their only duty is to cooperate in the cosmic play of the Divine and be blessed. This task has been admirably fulfilled by the book.
In the orthodox circles of राम devotees, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, is considered to be a mantraśāstra, a sacred book, each stanza of which is revered as a ‘mantra’ (mystic syllable) and devoutly repeated in a ceremonial way.
It is worthwhile noting that the well-known Hindi work, Rāmcaritamānas of Tulsīdas (A.

-1623), is based almost entirely on the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.
See also RĀMAGĪTĀ, RĀMAHṚDAYA and RĀMĀYAṆA.

adhyāropa
(‘superimposition’)
------------------------------------------
The attempts at reconciling ब्रह्मन् the Absolute with the world which is imperfect and limited have resulted in the ‘doctrine of अध्यारोप-अपवाद.’ The problem is sought to be resolved by considering the world as an अध्यारोप or अध्यास, a superimposition (even as a snake is superimposed on a rope resulting in illusory perception) and denying it absolute reality. The process of desuperimposition called ‘apavāda,’ consists of negating the illusory appearances by adopting the right means of knowledge and perceiving the truth as it is. अध्यारोप is practically the same as ‘adhyāsa’ (See ADHYĀSA.) A slight shade of difference in meaning is perhaps, that अध्यारोप refers to the process and अध्यास is the result.

adhyātmavidyā
(‘science pertaining to the Self within’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu sages have always advocated मोक्ष (liberation from transmi-gration) as the parama-puruṣārtha (the highest goal to be achieved by man) and have recommended अध्यात्मविद्या as the means of achieving it. अध्यात्मविद्या is the science that leads one to the realization of the Self within. It is the knowledge and wisdom taught in the उपनिषद्स्, the Bhagavadgītā and other works which follow them. A study of these books under enlightened teachers will lead to a clear understanding of the आत्मन् or the Self and meditation on this understanding will ultimately lead to realization. परा-विद्या and ब्रह्मविद्या are other words often used as synonyms for this. It is the highest knowledge and the only one worth seeking in life. Hence in the Bhagavadgītā, Lord कृष्ण goes to the extent of identifying himself with it (vide 10.31).

adhyātma-prasāda
(‘peace of the मिन्द् within’)
------------------------------------------
Mind is the basic instrument for gaining knowledge and wisdom. Controlling its vagaries and making it flow in a concentrated manner is the best means of attaining knowledge in any field. This however is easier said than done. By a long and arduous process of yogic discipline which includes the practice of ethical principles like अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truth) and ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and the practice of concentration by stages, the मिन्द् loses all its dross and impurities and becomes placid and pellucid. Such a state of मिन्द् is called ‘adhyātma-prasāda’ (vide Yogasūtras 1.47). In this state the मिन्द्, being rid of all impurities that distract and disturb it, has become like a pure crystal capable of reflecting the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the पुरुष (the Self), in full measure. Such a मिन्द् can produce instant knowledge of any object towards which it is directed.

adhyāsa
(‘superimposition’)
------------------------------------------
The Advaita Vedānta philosophy, the chief exponent of which was शङ्कर (A.

-820), accepts ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute), which is beyond names, forms, attributes, and hence, defies all description, as the Ultimate Reality. But the world that we perceive with its myriad names, forms and attributes, circumscribed by time, space and causation, cannot be easily brushed aside or wished away. Hence there is a great need to explain the relationship between ब्रह्मन् the Absolute and this world of phenomena. ‘Adhyāsa’ or ‘adhyāropa’ is the explanation offered by Advaita Vedānta.
Literally, the word means one thing ‘sitting upon’ another, hiding its nature for the time being. It is defined as ‘the appearance elsewhere, as in memory, of something perceived earlier.’ (Adhyāsa-bhāṣya of शङ्कर, Brahmasūtras

adhyayana
(‘studying and teaching’)
------------------------------------------
Study of the वेदस्, technically termed ‘adhyayana,’ was considered not only as part of एदुचतिओन् but as part of religious life as well. Since a change of स्वर (intonation) would often entail a change of meaning as well, great care was exercised in preserving the oral musical tradition of the वेदस्.
The student desirous of learning the वेदस् had to live in the होउसे of the गुरु, after first completing the sacrament of उपनयन. Avoiding the days known as ‘anadhyayana’ (or अनध्याय) (See ANADHYĀYA.) on all other permissible days he could approach the गुरु for Vedic studies after finishing the daily religious chores like the सन्ध्या. He had to sit facing north. The गुरु would recite the Vedic mantras pāda by pāda (i.e., a quarter of a stanza) and the student had to repeat them at least twice. Once he learnt the correct pronunciation and intonation and also committed it to memory, the गुरु would proceed with the next part. The student had to revise the lessons by himself or with the help of senior students the same day. The study would cover the Saṁhitā, the ब्राह्मण and the Upaniṣad parts of the particular śākhā (branch) of the Veda to which the student belonged. It would normally take twelve years to master one’s śākhā.
Along with the Vedic studies, a study of the वेदाङ्गस् (subsidiaries like grammar) धर्मशास्त्रस्, itihāsas and पुराणस् as also some secular sciences would also be pursued.
As for teaching (adhyāpana), it was expected that the teacher (adhyāpaka or आचार्य) should be well-versed and competent and of a sinless life. He could teach anyone eligible for Vedic studies, on any of the following three conditions:
as धर्म, as part of his duties;
for अर्थ or wealth, if the student promised it beforehand;
as a reward for śuśrūṣā or personal service. He was not expected to teach if none of these conditions was fulfilled.

adhyātma
(‘pertaining to the आत्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
In the उपनिषद्स् as well as in the Bhagavadgītā the three words adhibhūta, adhidaiva and अध्यात्म are frequently met with. The indeclinable ‘adhi’ has the sense of ‘ruling over,’ ‘pertaining to’. The word ‘ātman’ is often used in the sense of the body. Hence ‘adhyātma’ generally indicates the Self within the body which resides in it and rules over it. It is also used to indicate ब्रह्मन् or the Supreme Self.
The word is also used as an adjective and in combination with other words. For instance: अध्यात्मविद्या (knowledge of the Self), adhyātmayoga (yoga or meditation on the Self).
